A coverage-hole analysis shows fewer uncovered pixels than both baselines under high-resolution re-rendering.

papers.title: AI agents can redesign engineering parts with more than a thousand CAD parameters and nonlinear simulations
papers.authors: Alexandra Starostina; Alexander Hermann; Mahish Guru; Kartik Bali; Roland Aydin et al.
papers.abstract: Simulation-driven design of real engineering components has to meet three conditions at once. It runs on few solves, since a nonlinear finite-element simulation of a 3D part takes hours; its design space has many values, the hundreds to thousands of values of the part's CAD model; and a better design often needs a redesign, coordinated changes of the part's proportions rather than local polishing of its surface. Automated optimisers meet at most two of these conditions. Classical optimisers, Bayesian or derivative-free, need a person to cut the design down to a few parameters, and on all the values they need far more solves; industrial shape optimisers move every surface node of the mesh in one solve per cycle, but only in small steps that polish rather than redesign. We ask whether a general-purpose large language model (LLM) can meet all three by joining what it knows with what the simulation shows. GPT-6 Astra edits a magnesium stent through a CAD geometry parametrisation of about 1,650 values, with a budget of 15 simulations; every proposal is built in CAD, meshed and simulated with large-deformation plasticity and contact, and the LLM reads the full results of every solve. Within that budget it lowered the objective, a high percentile of the strains in the stent's bends, by 32%; on the same budget, the industrial shape optimiser Tosca improved the original design by a tenth and then stopped improving. An earlier GPT-6 Astra design, 25% lower in the same objective, was checked in an independent, higher-fidelity model of the full deployment with crimping and damage: it was 14% less strained than the original after the full chain, and its most damaged spot began to fail later and carried 63% less damage at full expansion. LLMs can thus join their learned knowledge with simulation data to adjust more than a thousand design values and reach valid designs with real improvements.

papers.title: The Csisz{á}r order for ranking the importance of input random variables
papers.authors: Cristina Butucea; Jean-François Delmas; Anne Dutfoy; Antoine Schoonaert
papers.abstract: Csisz{á}r indices $S\_f(X,Y)$, defined as the $f$-divergence between the joint distribution of a general random couple $(X,Y)$ and the product of its marginal distributions, are widely used to quantify dependence between the input variable $X$ and the output variable $Y$. We show that the ranking of two input variables $X$ and $X'$ in terms of their importance w.r.t.\ the output variable, given by the comparison of the Csisz{á}r indices $S\_f(X,Y)$ and $S\_f(X',Y)$ depends on the choice of $f$. We introduce the Csisz{á}r order of input variables as the uniform ordering of Csisz{á}r indices over all proper convex functions $f$. We give a sufficient condition to prove Csiszár order of two input multivariate random variables. We fully characterize it in two cases: when $(X,X',Y)$ is a Gaussian vector (in the one-dimensional case this amount to compare the square of their correlation); and when $X$, $X'$ and $Y$ are Bernoulli random variables. Finally, motivated by sensitivity analysis, we show that, when $(X,X',Y)$ is a three-dimensional Gaussian random vector, thresholding $X$, $X'$, and $Y$ either preserves the Csisz{á}r order or makes the input variables incomparable; in particular thresholding never reverses the ranking.

papers.title: Multi-View Transformer with Geometry-Guided Multi-Modal ControlNet for 3D Virtual Try-On
papers.authors: Sarthak Batra; Armin Mustafa; Adrian Hilton
papers.abstract: Editing a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) capture of a person so that they wear a new garment requires every rendered view to agree on the same garment details. Existing 3D virtual try-on (VTON) pipelines, however, edit training views largely independently and fuse them with hand-designed heuristics such as manually chosen reference views and fixed attention-blending weights. The resulting inconsistencies are baked into the 3D representation and surface as texture drift, blurred prints, and implausible geometry in novel views. We present GS-VTON-MVT, a three-stage framework that combines implicit and explicit 3D reasoning for consistent 3DGS try-on. (i) A multi-view inpainting transformer jointly edits a set of training views with full cross-view self-attention, so that cross-view correspondence is learned rather than imposed. (ii) A geometry-guided multi-modal ControlNet conditions the diffusion editor on the garment image together with depth and surface normals rendered from the current 3DGS state, supplying explicit structure where visual evidence is weakest. (iii) A pose-adaptive persona-aware attention replaces the fixed blending weight between current-view and reference-view features with weights derived from camera-pose proximity. On the 3D-VTONBench benchmark, GS-VTON-MVT improves FID, KID, LPIPS-based cross-view consistency, and user preference over general-purpose 3D editors and prior 3D try-on methods.

papers.title: Safe Data-Driven Insulin Dosage Decision Based on Physiology-Constrained Gaussian Process Learning
papers.authors: Deheng Cai; Xiang Lu; Wei Liu; Jing Chen; Linong Ji et al.
papers.abstract: Multiple daily injections (MDI) therapy is widely adopted by insulin-treated subjects with diabetes mellitus. In this work, we study how to ensure that data-driven model learning is aligned with the underlying physiological principles, and introduce a safe data-driven learning and decision framework for the MDI therapy. To provide credible glucose predictions for the decision, a physiology-constrained Gaussian process learning method is developed for glycemic dynamics modeling by encoding the physiological priors as constraints in the model training. Considering the natural day-to-day cycle of insulin decisions, a prediction-based optimization formulation with an objective function that has a penalty term associated with the previous dosage is employed for the insulin therapy, together with the asymmetric penalties on hyper- and hypoglycemia for safety. The effectiveness of the proposed method is verified using the 10-adult cohort from the FDA-accepted UVA/Padova T1DM simulator, and an advisory mode analysis is also conducted based on the clinical data from 40 type 1 diabetes and 55 type 2 diabetes subjects to indicate the safe and physiologically plausible decisions in the real-life applications.

papers.title: Optimal long-time derivative estimates for underdamped Langevin dynamics
papers.authors: Lukang Sun
papers.abstract: We study the long-time behaviour of derivatives of the semigroup $P_t=e^{t\mathcal{A}}$ generated by the underdamped Langevin (kinetic Fokker-Planck) operator $\mathcal{A}$ on $L^2(μ)$, where the Gibbs measure $μ$ is not required to be finite. Under a weighted relative bound on the Hessian of the potential, we prove that for every integer $m\ge 0$ the squared $L^2(μ)$ norms of $\mathcal{A}^m P_t h_0$ and of $\nabla_{x,v}\mathcal{A}^m P_t h_0$ are bounded by $C_m t^{-2m}\|h_0\|^2$ and $D_m t^{-(2m+1)}\|h_0\|^2$ respectively for large times, and the free dynamics shows that these exponents are optimal. The proof rests on a resolvent estimate near the imaginary axis, valid for every smooth potential, which follows from the adjoint relation between the generator and the velocity reversal and from the Gaussian Poincaré inequality in the velocity variable.

papers.title: GaussTrans: A Gaussian Interface Framework for Multi-Layer Refractive Transport
papers.authors: Zixuan Zhao; Tao Wang
papers.abstract: We investigate surface modeling of multi-transparent interfaces to achieve accurate light transmission. The interplay of errors in geometric structure, light paths, and observation results during the reconstruction of transparent media with a high number of layers makes this a challenging problem. Some existing techniques address the reconstruction of transparent scenes by reducing the number of layers or simplifying light paths; however, this limits their direct applicability to high-order transparent scenes. We propose GaussTrans, a compact framework for light transport in high-order transparent scenes, consisting of three components: Gaussian-Field Hybrid Surfaces, Transport-Coupled Refinement, and Primitive-Guided Implicit Intersection. Gaussian-Field Hybrid Surfaces use a hybrid approach combining Gauss surfaces and fields to reconstruct different interfaces. Transport-Coupled Refinement reduces coupling errors by evaluating the entire light path. Primitive-Guided Implicit Intersection combines primitive support regions to reduce errors in the intersection of interfaces and rays. In experiments on datasets such as RefRef, GaussTrans achieves significantly higher accuracy with relatively low spatial storage requirements.

papers.title: Spatio-Temporal Evolution of a Steady Transition Region Downflow above a Sunspot
papers.authors: Bablu Mandal; S. Krishna Prasad; Avijeet Prasad; Ambrish Pandey
papers.abstract: Super-Sonic Downflows (SSDs) are usually observed above sunspots as redshifted peaks in lower Transition Region (TR) spectral lines and can last from a few minutes to several hours. Utilising high-cadence, $\sim$3 hour long repeated-raster mode observations from Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph (IRIS), we investigate the spatio-temporal dynamics of such a downflow event above NOAA active region 12135. Triple Gaussian fitting to TR spectral lines, along with Non-Force Free Field (NFFF) extrapolation and Differential Emission Measure (DEM) analysis, is performed to study this event. Downflow is initially observed in both the umbral and penumbral regions. Over time, the penumbral downflow fades, while the umbral downflow strengthens and appears as a single structure initially but eventually splits into two spatial segments. The calculated average properties, including downflow speed, electron density, and mass flux for this event, align with established studies. Simultaneous evolution in overlying coronal loops is also observed using imaging data from the Atmospheric Imaging Assembly (AIA). DEM analysis of the coronal emission over the downflow region indicates corresponding changes in cool ($\log_{10}[T/\mathrm{K}] \in [5.5, 5.6]$) coronal plasma. As suggested by recurrent transient brightenings observed in the nearby region in coronal channels and the corresponding fan-spine magnetic topology identified from NFFF extrapolations, magnetic reconnection occurring in this region is proposed to be the cause of this evolution. Our analysis revealed that changes in the morphology of TR downflows are closely associated with evolution of overlying coronal loops.

papers.title: Point Dynamics as Proxy for Robotic World Models
papers.authors: Dong An; Tianyu Liu; Haoran Ding; Wen Yang; Anqing Duan et al.
papers.abstract: Robotic world models predict future video frames from the current observation and a sequence of robot actions. While recent models follow the given actions closely, manipulated objects often collapse or move inconsistently with the action. We attribute this to the conditioning: an action, or a rendering of the robot, specifies where the robot goes but not how the scene responds, leaving a single video model to infer the interaction dynamics implicitly while also rendering appearance. We therefore separate dynamics prediction from visual rendering, with 3D point dynamics as the proxy between them. Specifically, we lift the first frame into 3D points, simulate how they respond to the robot's motion with a learned point dynamics model, and render the simulated points back into pixel-aligned videos that any video model can read. In controlled experiments on the DROID dataset with two video renderers of different architectures, this point dynamics proxy reduces object motion error by 8.6% and 6.2% without degrading image quality, and by 8.1% on a real bimanual robot. Moreover, the video follows the simulation: more accurate dynamics yield more accurate object motion, and editing the points steers the video. This suggests that advances in dynamics modeling can translate into more faithful robotic world models.

papers.title: AGSR: Aperture-Guided Super-Resolution for Gaussian Splatting
papers.authors: Ayman Alkhateeb; Hadi Amirpour; Christian Timmerer
papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables real-time novel view synthesis, but Gaussian rasterization attenuates fine-scale scene structure through the projected covariance of each primitive. We show that contracting these projected covariances at inference time can mitigate the effective bandwidth limitation induced by finite Gaussian footprints, motivating a multi-aperture rendering framework for super-resolution.   Based on this insight, we propose AGSR (Aperture-Guided Super-Resolution), a lightweight inference-time framework that progressively fuses multi-aperture renderings using uncertainty-guided feature aggregation and geometric conditioning from transmittance and depth cues. AGSR operates as a plug-in enhancement for pre-trained 3DGS models.   Experiments on the Mip-NeRF 360 benchmark show that AGSR outperforms lightweight image-space super-resolution baselines, with gains increasing as the underlying Gaussian representation deteriorates. The results provide evidence that covariance contraction exposes bandwidth-sensitive structural cues attenuated by native Gaussian rasterization. AGSR achieves these improvements while maintaining real-time performance with up to 139k parameters.

papers.title: Interpretation of the LZ Event via Inelastic ALP-Dark Photon Transition with Photon Exchange
papers.authors: Quanyu Wang; Xiangwei Yin; Tianjun Li
papers.abstract: The LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) experiment has reported a nuclear recoil event at $248\pm23$~keV with a global significance of about $2.6σ$. We for the first time explain it via the inelastic process with photon mediator. We consider a dark matter (DM) axion-like particle (ALP) $a$ converts into a heavier dark photon $γ'$ via the nuclear electromagnetic current, and study the photon-mediated endothermic transition $aA\rightarrowγ'A$. We derive the kinematics and cross sections for non-relativistic halo and boosted ALPs. A three-bin Poisson fit to the LZ data includes the xenon isotopes, charge form factors, detector efficiency, and energy resolution. Halo DM, which has mass $m\simeq1.2$~TeV, mass splitting $δ\simeq346$~keV, and near the upper coupling bound, reproduces the event with about $61\%$ in the middle bin. Boosted DM with $v_{0}=0.05\,c$ and $Φ_{0}=10^{5}~\mathrm{cm^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$ requires only $m\simeq5.74$~GeV and $δ\simeq6.66$~MeV to give about $62\%$. We find that a broader Gaussian spread in the incident energy has a significant effect on the fitted masses.

papers.title: Why Flat Drafts Stay Flat: Region-Mean Latents Govern Texture in Flow-Based Image Generation
papers.authors: Zihan Gu; Jiangcan Jia; Hua Zhang; Lulu Zhao
papers.abstract: Flat color-block drafts specify layout and regional color while leaving interior detail unspecified, yet pretrained flow-based generators can preserve their flat appearance even under photorealistic prompts. We trace this behavior to a cross-scale mechanism linking fine pixel variation to regional means in variational autoencoder (VAE) latent space. Flattening photo regions systematically shifts their latent means, with offsets concentrated along a shared channel direction within each backbone. Controlled field exchanges in FLUX.1-dev and Qwen-Image establish the effect of this displacement on texture generation: adding the photo-derived regional mean field to a flat latent restores texture, whereas adding its complementary field alone largely preserves flatness. A second-order encoding expansion explains how encoder curvature can convert zero-mean perturbations into mean shifts. An analytically solvable conditional Gaussian flow shows how regional noise averaging enables near-unit endpoint sensitivity at high signal-to-noise ratios. This mechanism motivates training-free rendering through pixel dither before encoding, mean-field scaling, and early boundary holding. Paired low-rank adaptation (LoRA) with draft conditioning improves content recovery and produces photo-like regional means under the standard velocity objective. Explicit regional mean guidance remains effective after adaptation, continuously controlling texture and improving color fidelity. These findings connect encoding shifts to persistent generation behavior and support interventions evaluated for texture, spatial fidelity, and semantic recovery.

papers.title: Time-independent equivalent matrix representation for time-domain boundary element analysis of large-scale 3D acoustic problems
papers.authors: Weiyu Zhou; Yongqiang Chen
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a time-independent equivalent matrix representation for large-scale three-dimensional (3D) acoustic analysis with the time-domain boundary element method (TDBEM). In conventional TDBEM, pair-dependent retarded times couple spatial interactions to historical boundary data, causing substantial storage and history-convolution costs. The proposed representation decouples compressible spatial interactions from propagation history, allowing reuse of the same compressed spatial representation across propagation delays and throughout time marching without additional temporal interpolation of the kernel. For conventional space-time discretizations, blockwise low-rank compression yields the compressed equivalent matrix method in the $\mathcal{H}$-matrix format (CEM-$\mathcal{H}$), with dynamic cluster-pair tracking to skip inactive interactions during wavefront propagation. For low-frequency, long-wavelength problems with a bounded number of nonzero time-lag matrices, the framework is extended to the $\mathcal{H}^2$-matrix format (CEM-$\mathcal{H}^2$) using delay-consistent partitioning, shared coupling matrices, and nested cluster bases. Under sparsity and bounded-parameter assumptions, storage and per-step cost of CEM-$\mathcal{H}^2$ both scale as $O(N_s)$, excluding preprocessing. Numerical results agree well with conventional TDBEM and semi-analytical reference solutions. For CEM-$\mathcal{H}$, the storage requirement for a sphere with $N_s=20,480$ is reduced from approximately 349.0 GB to 1.6 GB, with a speedup of approximately $45.4\times$. For CEM-$\mathcal{H}^2$, simulations with up to $N_s=1,310,720$ are performed in the low-frequency, long-wavelength regime. A million-degree-of-freedom underwater-vehicle model is also analyzed. These results demonstrate the capability of the proposed framework for large-scale 3D transient acoustic analysis using TDBEM.

papers.title: Inference in High-Dimensional Linear Mediation Models
papers.authors: Samriddha Lahiry; Rajarshi Mukherjee; Pragya Sur
papers.abstract: Mediation analysis plays an important role in psychology, epidemiology, and genomics. Al- though high-dimensional mediation has been studied extensively, existing inferential methods typically rely on sparsity assumptions that may be difficult to justify when many individually weak mediators collectively produce a substantial effect. We study inference for both the over- all indirect effect and the effect transmitted through an individual mediator in a proportional high-dimensional regime, where the number of mediators and the sample size grow at compa- rable rates, without imposing sparsity on the mediator effects. Standard debiasing procedures for high-dimensional inference commonly rely on design-covariance information or additional structural assumptions on precision-matrix directions. In mediation models, however, the full outcome-design covariance depends on unknown mediator-model coefficients, creating an addi- tional challenge when such information or structure is unavailable. To address this challenge, we introduce an approximate debiasing procedure based on partial ridge regression and show that the resulting estimator is asymptotically bias-corrected and Gaussian. We also develop a cross-fitted estimator with a smaller asymptotic variance than its sample-split counterpart. In addition, we construct consistent estimators of the limiting variances of both the sample-split and cross-fitted estimators. Together, these results provide feasible inferential procedures for global and pathwise mediation effects.

papers.title: Microscopic Probabilities for U-Statistics and Almost-Balanced Permutations
papers.authors: Hillel Schein
papers.abstract: We estimate the probability that a vector of U-statistics lies within $C/n$ of a target in the range of typical fluctuations. For sufficiently large $C$, we prove a lower bound of the typical Gaussian order under finite variance, and a matching upper bound for bounded kernels. We show that under finite variance alone, stronger concentration may occur, and find the best possible asymptotic upper bound. Our proof is algorithmic, estimating probabilities by counting successful modifications produced by a random algorithm.   We apply this result to settle a question of Beniamini, Lavee and Linial (2025), who asked if there exist permutations with $k$-order sub-pattern counts at most $O(n^{k-1})$ away from one another for $k>4$. We prove not only existence, but enumerate these permutations up to a constant factor, showing that there are $Θ(n!n^{-(k-1)^2/2})$ such permutations of size $n$.

papers.title: SCCV-6D: Sparse Canonical Coordinate Voting for Holistic Multi-View RGB-D 6D Pose Estimation in Robotic Bin Picking
papers.authors: Nico Leuze; Samed Dogan; Maximilian Hoh; Henry Schaub; Alfred Schöttl
papers.abstract: Industrial bin picking requires pose estimates that are accurate under clutter, partial occlusion, and the reflective, texture-less nature of manufactured parts. Most recent approaches to 6D pose estimation follow multi-stage pipelines. These achieve high accuracy, but incur memory and runtime footprints that do not cope with the operational constraints of many real-world industrial deployments. Holistic pipelines estimate poses in a single pass, with cost controlled through indiscriminate subsampling or lowered resolution. Continuing this line, we present SCCV-6D, a fully sparse multi-view RGB-D estimator. We reconstruct the 3D space at millimeter precision, prune background via a staged heatmap mechanism, and predict class, translation offset and rotation at highest resolution for an arbitrary number of objects simultaneously. Rotation is formulated as canonical coordinate voting. Points vote for their canonical object coordinates with an associated confidence, enabling closed-form pose recovery with a symmetry-aware weighted Procrustes solve. Along an in-cluster point recovery induced by offset votes, this removes time-consuming post-processing stages. We reuse the task-supervised attention priors from the heatmap formulation for a novel attention-gated distillation objective that reweights teacher-student feature alignment. On the IPD test split we report competitive 0.826 AP at 1.13 s per scene, significantly faster than the leading entries. On MV-YCB our approach reaches 96.1 ADD-S, and remains competitive even on the densely packed bins of ROBI.

papers.title: World-delta: Continually Integrating Observations for Incremental 3D Scene Generation
papers.authors: Haonan Wang; Hanyu Zhou; Xiaobin Hu; Luxin Yan
papers.abstract: Existing 3D generation methods synthesize visually compelling scenes from fixed inputs, yet struggle to continually expand and revise a 3D world as new observations arrive. Iterative approaches often fuse real observations and generated content into a single representation, treating generated content as established structure rather than revisable predictions. Consequently, early generation errors can persist and accumulate despite new evidence. We propose World-delta, an incremental 3D scene generation framework combining uncertainty-aware persistent world modeling with delta-guided diffusion for continual scene expansion and correction. Our framework comprises three components: 1) Visual Evidence Encoding integrates geometric and semantic cues from incoming images into unified world tokens. 2) Observation-Calibrated World Modeling maintains a persistent latent world state that distinguishes observation-supported content from provisional completion hypotheses. New evidence drives selective world deltas to revise conflicting hypotheses while preserving well-supported content. 3) Incremental World Diffusion Generation uses delta-derived masks to restrict diffusion to regions requiring updates, freezing unchanged regions. Only affected 3D chunks are decoded and integrated into the existing scene. Together, these components enable continual world expansion and revision while reducing redundant generation and preserving scene consistency. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of World-delta in incremental 3D scene generation, observation-driven correction, scene consistency, and update efficiency over successive scene updates.

papers.title: Fast and Accurate Body Estimation in Pixels, World Space and Scenes
papers.authors: Jinkun Cao
papers.abstract: We present FAB (Fast and Accurate Body estimation), a human body estimator that jointly improves inference efficiency and body-recovery fidelity. Rather than predicting only parametric mesh-model parameters, FAB directly predicts human skeleton joints and dense surface points. In images, it predicts dense 2D and 3D body points alongside a parametric Momentum Human Rig (MHR) head, then fits SMPL in one learned pass followed by two Gauss-Newton steps. Its ViT-L student, FAB-L, distilled from a fine-tuned SAM 3D Body, runs in real time for one person on an RTX 4070 Ti SUPER, from detection to a fitted body, at 4.6x the speed of SAM 3D Body's eager-PyTorch body-only path, while improving accuracy on most camera-space benchmarks. The same network predicts heel, toe, hand, and knee contacts, which connect the body to the scene. FAB also estimates world-space motion, fuses static-scene depth around the visible person, and aligns body and scene using predicted contacts. For human-to-humanoid real-to-sim transfer, an in-model G1 head and FAB-Retarget, a motion-level retargeter that reads dense points or the fitted mesh, map motion to a Unitree G1. FAB-Retarget produces references that follow the person more closely than specialized retargeters including SOMA, GMR, UMR, and OmniRetarget, and substantially more closely than Fast SAM 3D Body retargeted with our sequence IK. Project page: https://www.jinkuncao.com/FAB.

papers.title: GeoPillars: A Large-Kernel Pillar Detector for Single-Sweep LiDAR Under Point Sparsity, and a Decomposition of Its Gain
papers.authors: Chaitanya Dumbre; Shubham Sarkar; Akash Mohapatra; Ghanasham Patil; Sheetal Girase
papers.abstract: GeoPillars is a pillar-based 3D detector for single-sweep LiDAR under a hard budget of eight points per 0.4 m pillar, a budget that discards 46.6% of in-range points. It adds geometric pillar features, grouped vector attention within each pillar, a learned absolute positional prior on the bird's-eye-view (BEV) grid, a large-kernel backbone, auxiliary surface-normal supervision and a full-resolution detection head. Trained on 123k synthetic CARLA scans and evaluated on cars, it reaches 81.33 BEV AP@0.7, 13.76 points above CenterPoint at the same input budget and 1.91 points above CenterPoint at its native, denser budget. These are in-distribution figures, because the validation split is per-frame rather than scene-disjoint. A rung-by-rung decomposition shows that the new components explain little of the gain. Raising the detection-head resolution alone recovers 10.19 of the 13.76 points, the joint change of encoder, backbone, neck and positional prior adds 3.37, and the normal-supervision branch adds 0.20, which is within run-to-run variation. With heading reversals folded out, orientation error is similar for all seven models, although GeoPillars reverses headings about half as often as a resolution-matched baseline. It is also the slowest of the seven models. Evaluated zero-shot on 6,743 real nuScenes keyframes, no model transfers, and each retains 3.7% to 12.2% of its CARLA accuracy. A collection defect left LiDAR intensity constant, so every model learned from geometry alone. Code and checkpoints are publicly available.

papers.title: Trading Before a Committed Rebalance
papers.authors: Khizar Qureshi
papers.abstract: An institution must complete a portfolio adjustment, but traders who prepare inventory for it can choose whether to participate. We study how public forecasts affect the institution's cost in a Bayesian execution game with optional activation, transient impact, and uniform-price terminal completion. The curvature of equilibrium cost as a function of the posterior target mean determines the value of information. In the scalar model, information benefits every fixed participation roster. Optional supply can reverse this ranking at entry, at full participation, and in a smooth interior with lognormal activation costs. For centered scalar targets, information weakly lowers cost relative to no information, strictly when the posterior mean is nonzero with positive probability. Centered Gaussian precision gains are always beneficial. An exact symmetric finite-population equilibrium identifies how information resolution and individual strategic size interact near entry. A portfolio extension gives a matrix criterion for the fixed-roster ranking, which can fail under general cross-impact. Even with isotropic execution, shared activation allows equally accurate signals about target magnitude and composition to have opposite execution values under one unchanged prior. Intraday ETF price data is used to characterize target uncertainty and trading conditions without identifying activation or institutional costs.

papers.title: DACA: Dual-Anchor Collaborative Agent for Zero-Shot 3D Visual Grounding
papers.authors: Jiaming Liu; Linghe Kong; Guixu Zhang; Huaxi Huang
papers.abstract: 3D visual grounding (3D-VG) is a task that bridges the natural language and 3D space, serving as a foundational capability for embodied intelligence and human-computer interaction. Although recent 3D-VG agents overcome the reliance on pre-processed 3D point clouds, they essentially employ a unidirectional, pipeline-style tool-calling architecture. This architecture separates semantic understanding from geometric reconstruction, leading to error accumulation and an inability to autonomously recover from failures. To address this flaw, this paper proposes the Dual-Anchor Collaborative Agent (DACA), which reinterprets 3D-VG as a semantic-geometric dual-anchor collaborative reasoning paradigm. DACA comprises two complementary specialized tools: the semantic anchor tool holds the visual semantic features of the target and achieves efficient target tracking via optical flow and VLM local verification; the geometric anchor tool holds the 3D spatial geometric features of the target and performs global spatial reasoning via voxelization and multi-keypoint projection. The two components exchange information bidirectionally via a standardized tool call protocol, autonomously deciding on the next perception-action step to form a closed-loop optimization. Experiments on the ScanRefer and Nr3D benchmarks demonstrate that zero-shot DACA achieves an overall Acc@0.25 of 73.6\% on ScanRefer and 70.4\% overall accuracy on Nr3D, far surpassing the latest zero-shot 3D-VG methods. The code and models are available at https://github.com/liujia99/DACA

papers.title: LIFT: Lifting Language-Controlled Image Fusion to Free-Viewpoint 3D Scenes
papers.authors: Jingning Tian; Hao Zhang; Yumin Huang; Zizhuo Li; Xingyu Jiang et al.
papers.abstract: Multimodal image fusion traditionally generates a single fused image from paired observations at a specific viewpoint, limiting comprehensive scene perception and adaptability to diverse perceptual objectives. To overcome these limitations, we present LIFT, a novel framework for our proposed language-controlled 3D image fusion (L3D-IF) paradigm that extends multimodal image fusion from 2D images to free-viewpoint 3D scenes, enabling language-guided fusion tailored to diverse perceptual objectives. First, LIFT formulates Semantic Modality Binding (SMB), which interprets language instructions to identify semantic targets and their associated modality preferences and grounds these targets in corresponding regions of a shared Gaussian scene, establishing persistent semantic-to-spatial correspondences for consistent fusion control across viewpoints. Second, Language-Conditioned Gaussian Appearance (LCGA) is developed to achieve scene-wide multimodal appearance modeling by combining adaptive multimodal blending with language- and viewpoint-conditioned appearance refinement, enabling spatially adaptive realization of diverse fusion appearances while preserving source fidelity at pure-modality endpoints. Finally, we construct a Multi-View Language-Supervision (MVLS) dataset that associates language instructions and calibrated viewpoints with modulated fused images, providing effective supervision for learning instruction-dependent fusion from finite multi-view observations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LIFT achieves coherent multimodal fusion across continuous viewpoints, accurate semantic target localization, and consistent regional fusion control under diverse language instructions.

papers.title: Energy transfers in decaying three-dimensional Hall-magnetohydrodynamics turbulence: Dependence on the Ion-Inertial Length and the Magnetic Prandtl Number
papers.authors: Pratik Patel; Sharad K. Yadav; Akanksha Gupta; Hideaki Miura; Rahul Pandit
papers.abstract: We present a systematic study of energy transfers in three-dimensional (3D) decaying Hall-magnetohydrodynamics (HMHD) turbulence. Our study has been designed to investigate the dependence of these transfers on initial energy spectra, the ion-inertial length $d_{i}$, and the magnetic Prandtl number $Pr_{m}$. Using shell-to-shell decomposition, we compute the energy transfer rates for (a) kinetic-to-kinetic, (b) magnetic-to-magnetic, (c) kinetic-to-magnetic, and (d) magnetic-to-kinetic interactions by carrying out extensive pseudospectral direct numerical simulations (DNSs) of 3D HMHD and its MHD counterpart. Furthermore, we examine the magnetic-to-magnetic and current-density-to-magnetic energy transfers arising from the Hall term in this framework. Energy transfers between like fields -- namely, kinetic-to-kinetic and magnetic-to-magnetic -- are predominantly local and forward in direction, cascading energy from large to small length scales. This behavior is consistent with a self-similar flow structure in the inertial range. Cross-field transfers, between kinetic and magnetic energy, are found to be forward but non-local in character. At low and high $Pr_{m}$, the transfers become local, and the nonlinear energy transfer is significantly suppressed. Moreover, we observe that the Hall term drives both inverse and forward transfers of magnetic energy, associated with local and non-local transfer, respectively.

papers.title: GNetSS: Towards Learning GNSS Corrections without Ground Truth
papers.authors: JiaXu Chee; Simon Denman; Fahira Afzal Maken; Qingqing Cheng; Amir Khodabandeh et al.
papers.abstract: We present GNetSS, a self-supervised GNSS position correction framework that improves the robustness of single point positioning (SPP) without requiring ground-truth locations for training. GNetSS combines a transformer-based network with a deterministic differentiable positioning solver. The network predicts satellite-wise pseudorange corrections by modelling inter-satellite geometry and temporal context, while the solver converts these corrected measurements into receiver position corrections under GNSS geometry and optional motion constraints. Unlike supervised GNSS correction methods that rely on ground-truth, GNetSS derives its training signal directly from GNSS measurement consistency. Experimental results show that GNetSS improves robustness across open-sky, urban, and forested environments. The method is particularly effective at suppressing large-error outliers, reducing the maximum 3D positioning error by over 50% compared with SPP. These results demonstrate the potential of self-supervised pseudorange correction for scalable and robust GNSS positioning in real-world autonomy applications. Code and the in-house dataset will be released upon acceptance.

papers.title: DAWN: Robust Neural Blind Deconvolution via Alternating Wiener Guidance
papers.authors: Yida Pan; Yixuan Jia; Chaoyan Huang; Qing Qu; Ismail Alkhouri
papers.abstract: Blind image deconvolution (BID) is an ill-posed inverse problem that aims to jointly recover a sharp image and blur kernel from a single degraded observation. Under nontrivial and high noise, which is common in photography and scientific imaging such as microscopy, BID remains particularly challenging, as existing methods suffer from noise overfitting and inaccurate kernel estimation. Existing training-data-free learning methods for BID, such as those based on the deep image prior (DIP), often utilize external guidance by including model-based estimates as additional loss terms, which underexploits the information these estimates carry especially under nontrivial noise. To address these challenges, we propose DAWN, a training-data-free DIP framework that alternates between injecting model-based estimates directly into the model input and refining this imperfect estimate with the network's own prior. To provide more reliable kernel estimates for these injections, we apply autoencoding regularization to both the image and kernel networks. On natural and scientific images under varying levels of Gaussian and Poisson noise, DAWN outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both image and kernel quality (achieving up to +4.5 dB over the next best baseline on the Levin dataset at $σ= 0.1$). Without any training images, DAWN remains highly competitive with a state-of-the-art diffusion model on FFHQ, despite the latter being trained on a massive number of in-distribution images.

papers.title: Onset of three dimensionality in transonic shock boundary layer interaction over a natural laminar flow airfoil
papers.authors: Abhijeet Guha; Aditi Sengupta
papers.abstract: The development of three-dimensionality in transonic shock--boundary-layer interactions (SBLI) can significantly influence the aerodynamic response of natural laminar flow (NLF) airfoils, yet the associated vorticity dynamics remain insufficiently understood. The present study investigates the short-time evolution of transonic SBLI over the SHM1 NLF airfoil using high-fidelity three-dimensional (3D) simulations at three operating conditions reported by Fujino et al., Natural-laminar-flow airfoil development for a lightweight business jet, J. Aircraft 40, 609-615 (2003). The selected cases represent three distinct operating regimes: the initial development of a normal shock, drag divergence, and shock-induced separation. Comparisons with previously reported two-dimensional (2D) simulations establish the temporal interval over which the spanwise-averaged 3D flow remains close to the corresponding 2D evolution, while departures in surface pressure and skin-friction responses identify the subsequent development of 3D effects within the SBLI region. The temporal evolution of volume-integrated streamwise and wall-normal enstrophies further characterizes the development of the associated 3D vortical field. The compressible enstrophy transport equation (CETE) is subsequently employed to examine the mechanisms governing the evolution of the 3D vortical field. Viscous and compressibility-related terms dominate the normalized enstrophy budget during the early evolution, while vortex stretching remains a minor contribution in the normal-shock and drag-divergence regimes but becomes appreciable, albeit intermittently, with the development of shock-induced separation. Across the three operating regimes, the same principal enstrophy-transport mechanisms remain active, but their relative contributions to the normalized budget are redistributed with the SBLI topology.

papers.title: Structure and Binding of the \texorpdfstring{$pnΩ^-$}{pnOmega} System with a Near-Unitary \texorpdfstring{$NΩ$}{NOmega} Interaction from Physical-Point Lattice QCD
papers.authors: Faisal Etminan
papers.abstract: The binding and spatial structure of the \(pnΩ^-\) system are investigated in the \(I(J^P)=0(5/2^+)\) channel using the physical-point HAL QCD \(NΩ({}^{5}S_2)\) interaction. The pairwise Hamiltonian includes the spin-triplet \(pn\) interaction and the finite-size Coulomb attraction in the \(pΩ^-\) pair. The three-body Schrödinger equation is solved with the Gaussian Expansion Method (GEM), including all three Jacobi rearrangement configurations. For the central HAL QCD potential at \(t/a=14\), the calculated three-body binding energy is \(18.63\) MeV, corresponding to a separation energy of \(16.39\) MeV relative to the \(d+Ω^-\) threshold. The spatial structure is examined through interparticle root-mean-square distances, pair and spectator radial distributions, and the correlation between the two Jacobi coordinates. Relative to a frozen-deuteron folded reference, the full three-body solution exhibits a substantially more compact spectator distribution and a contracted \(pn\) pair. The dependence on the Euclidean-time choice of the HAL QCD potential is also assessed. The results characterize the three-body rearrangement induced by the attractive \(NΩ\) interaction within the adopted pairwise model.

papers.title: Geometry-induced orientational trapping dictates escape of active rods in corrugated channels
papers.authors: Baburao Simma; Rahul Bag; Hari K. Reddy; Radha Ramana; Vrinda Garg et al.
papers.abstract: The non-equilibrium transport of anisotropic active matter through geometrically confined environments is fundamentally governed by the interplay between self-propulsion and geometry-induced entropic barriers. Using overdamped Langevin dynamics, we reveal contrasting escape mechanisms of self-driven rods in narrow corrugated channels by comparing smoothly varying sinusoidal (SC) geometries to circular (CC) cavities with localized, uniform curvature. We observe a strictly non-monotonic dependence of the mean first escape time (MFET) with increasing Peclet number (Pe) in the CC channel, contrary to the monotonic dependence in the SC channel. This non-monotonicity emerges from a competition between activity-enhanced escape at low-to-intermediate propulsion and persistent, geometry-induced orientational trapping along the circular boundary at high propulsion, which inhibits reorientation toward the exit neck. This regime crossover is further corroborated by trajectory-to-trajectory escape fluctuations and bimodal radial probability distributions reflecting persistent wall-collision and wall-aligned sliding transport. The self part of van-Hove correlation function exhibits distinct anisotropic non-Gaussian displacements in the SC channel, in contrast to symmetric profiles with extended active-trapping plateaus in the CC cavities. These results establish local channel topology as a critical determinant of confined active transport, with direct implications for microfluidic sorting, biological navigation, and targeted drug delivery in corrugated environments.

papers.title: Direct measurement of the on-shot focal-spot size of a kilojoule-class petawatt laser
papers.authors: Ryunosuke Takizawa; Keisuke Takahashi; Yuhei Kawakami; Hiroki Matsubara; Yuga Karaki et al.
papers.abstract: We report a direct, on-shot determination of the focal-spot size of a kilojoule-class, four-beam petawatt laser. Encircled-energy curves were inferred from the energy transmitted around aluminum-coated spheres of varying diameters placed at the focal plane. The 50% encircled-energy diameter D50 of each beam was obtained by fitting a two-component Gaussian mixture with Bayesian inference. With all deformable mirrors optimized in closed loop, the best-corrected alignment beam reached D50 = 34 (+4/-5) um, three times the diffraction limit of 10 um. Under full-power conditions, the thermal distortion of the main amplifier broadened this beam to D50 = 102 (+9/-8) um and reduced its peak intensity ninefold, to 2.2 (+0.6/-0.9) x 10^18 W/cm^2 at 250 J and 1.3 ps. The energy fraction of the narrow component decreased from 68% to 38%. These reference values serve facility users, and a deformable mirror upstream of the pulse compressor, now on one beam only, doubles the on-shot peak intensity.

papers.title: Efficient Multimodal Agents for Auditing 3D Worlds
papers.authors: Jingbo Yang; Ziyan Jiang; Li An; Jiabao Ji; Yujian Liu et al.
papers.abstract: Multimodal agents can now build interactive 3D worlds and games, yet these worlds, like those built by people, often contain glitches such as floating objects, walls that can be walked through, or objects that change when no one is looking. An automatic auditor could check such worlds at scale and provide rewards for agents that build them, but only if it is both accurate and cheap. Auditing requires three abilities, namely navigating to the objects that may contain a glitch, triggering glitches that appear only after a specific behavior, and recognizing what is wrong. Current auditors are either accurate but slow and expensive or cheap but unreliable. We study how much of the audit small models can take on. A 4B vision language model fine-tuned end to end on verified trajectories of a frontier teacher guided by Bayesian search learns to navigate and trigger, and six such explorers together match a frontier model on both, but recognition stays far behind. We therefore build an auditor in which a swarm of small explorers navigates and triggers, and a frontier model reviews what they record and report. On WorldAuditBench, our auditor succeeds on 55.9% of 213 tasks in Unreal Engine 5 and Three.js worlds, 13.6 points above the strongest auditor reported, at less than a quarter of its cost. It matches the frontier reviewer exploring on its own at 4.6 times lower cost and about half the latency. Without further training, it also answers embodied questions about real-world scans, matching the frontier reviewer exploring on its own and surpassing four other frontier models by 6.4 to 16.6 points.

papers.title: Differentially Private Score Estimation with Applications to Score-Based Generative Models
papers.authors: Mengxiao Gao; Elly K. H. Hung; Yuchen Wu; Yi Yu
papers.abstract: Estimating the score function of a distribution plays a central role in statistics and machine learning, with applications in distribution estimation, sampling, and score-based generative modeling. However, learning scores from sensitive data raises privacy concerns. These concerns are particularly pronounced in score-based generative modeling, where trained models may memorize individual training examples and expose sensitive information through membership inference and data extraction attacks.   Although non-private score estimation has been extensively studied, the statistical limits of its private counterpart remain less understood. In this work, we study score estimation under $(α,β)$-differential privacy for $d$-dimensional sub-Gaussian distributions with locally $γ$-Hölder-continuous scores. We develop a sampling-based private score estimator using quadratic B-splines and the exponential mechanism, and we implement our proposal through projected Langevin Monte Carlo with runtime polynomial in the sample size $n$. The proposed estimator satisfies $(α,β)$-differential privacy, and achieves expected density-weighted squared error $\mbox{polylog}(n) \max(n^{-2γ/(d+2γ+2)},\,(nα)^{-2γ/(d+γ+1)})$. We also establish a nearly matching private minimax lower bound, thereby characterizing the privacy-accuracy trade-off for score estimation. As an application, we construct a differentially private diffusion model whose privacy guarantee is independent of the number of denoising steps. We show that, with an appropriate discretization scheme, the resulting diffusion model attains nearly minimax optimal expected total variation error among all private distribution estimators. We validate our theoretical findings through experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

papers.title: Multi-View Relighting with Mergeable Radiance Fields
papers.authors: Yinan Wang; Rohan Kadkol; Hyunjin Yoo; Jean-François Lalonde; James J. Clark
papers.abstract: We propose MergeableRF, a method for radiance field relighting through model parameter merging. Given multi-view images of a scene under known basis lights, our goal is to relight the scene by directly combining the parameters of radiance fields trained under these lights. This is motivated by the linearity of light transport: the image under a mixture of lights is the same weighted combination of the images under each light. However, combining the parameters of independently trained radiance fields does not produce the corresponding combination of images. To address this, we represent a scene with shared geometry and a separate appearance network for each basis light. We start these networks from the same initialization and introduce merge-aware training, which teaches their parameter combinations to reproduce the corresponding combinations of images. Given a target HDR environment map, we compute its basis-light coefficients and use them to merge the appearance networks into a single relit model. Our method supports both Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), without material estimation, additional relighting networks, or target-specific optimization. Unlike image-space blending, it requires only one rendering pass per viewpoint. Experiments on synthetic Neural Gaffer objects and real OLATverse captures demonstrate relighting quality competitive with methods trained on the same multi-light observations.

papers.title: The computational complexity of bosonic Lindbladian fixed points
papers.authors: En-Jui Kuo; Arsalan Motamedi; Mohammad Hafezi; Saeed Mehraban
papers.abstract: We study the computational complexity of estimating observables and sampling from stationary states, or fixed points, of bosonic Lindbladian dynamics with bounded-degree polynomial interactions. While the complexity of transient bosonic dynamics has been investigated, understanding the computational power of bosonic fixed points requires addressing subtleties of infinite-dimensional systems, including the existence, uniqueness, and convergence of stationary states.   We establish a broad complexity landscape spanning universal quantum computation, efficient classical simulation, sampling hardness, and undecidability. First, we show that universal quantum computation can be embedded into observable estimation at the unique fixed point of a bosonic Lindbladian with a Hamiltonian of degree at most twelve and only linear photon loss. Moreover, this fixed point can be prepared from vacuum in polynomial time. On the classical side, we identify Gaussian regimes with incoherent pumping that admit efficient photon-number sampling and establish stability of classical approximability under sufficiently weak non-Gaussian Kerr perturbations. Conversely, for Gaussian fixed points without incoherent pumping, we establish hardness of exact sampling under constant-rate linear loss and hardness of approximate sampling at inverse-polynomial loss rates under standard boson-sampling conjectures. We also relate sampling from non-Gaussian fixed points to variants of boson sampling. Finally, we prove that deciding the existence of a stationary density operator is $\mathsf{RE}$-hard, even for purely dissipative Lindbladians with degree-five jump operators acting on at most four modes.

papers.title: Mesh-Free Keypoint Learning for Category-Level 6D Object Pose Estimation
papers.authors: Junghoon Seo; Hakjin Lee; Jaehoon Sim
papers.abstract: Category-level 6D pose estimation relates partial RGB-D observations of unseen instances to a canonical frame shared across a category. Object-aware reconstruction helps adaptive keypoints retain the geometry of the visible surface. Common reconstruction targets select observed points by their distance to a registered instance surface. We present MORSEPose, which derives this support directly from standard pose and metric-size annotations. We map observed 3D points to normalized object coordinates and retain those inside a tolerancedilated pose-and-size envelope. This construction is consistent across camera frames and metric scales. When the annotated extent bounds the object surface, the envelope conservatively contains the support of a conventional surface-distance selector. We integrate this target with multi-level RGB-D features, adaptive keypoints, and learnable category context. Experiments on REAL275 and HouseCat6D show that the envelope closely matches surface-based supervision at both point and task levels, remains stable under boundary perturbations and viewpoint changes, and supports competitive category-level pose accuracy across benchmarks.

papers.title: PRIO: Pre-trained Representation for Interactive Objects in 4D Worlds
papers.authors: Shixun Huang; Lifu Wei; Yue Chang; Chen Geng; Heng Zhang et al.
papers.abstract: 3D worlds can now be captured, reconstructed, and generated at scale, yet the objects in them stay still: a pressed pillow does not compress, and a pulled door does not swing. Bringing these objects into interactive 4D world models requires a representation of how they can move, deform, and respond physically to user actions in real time. We present PRIO, a pre-trained representation for interactive objects. Given static geometry, PRIO predicts an object-specific configuration space in a single forward pass. This space provides generalized coordinates for Lagrangian mechanics, allowing physical laws and user actions to govern motion. Configurations are linear in these coordinates, allowing the quantities needed by the dynamics to be precomputed. Dynamics then run at interactive rates without further network inference. Pre-trained on diverse 4D trajectories, PRIO learns priors over object configurations that generalize to unseen shapes. It supports meshes, point clouds, and 3D Gaussians, bringing objects in reconstructed and generated scenes into interaction. We demonstrate its use in real-to-sim workflows and robot manipulation. In addition, compared with existing 4D generation methods, PRIO generates dynamics faster and follows user actions more faithfully.

papers.title: Convex splitting by binary quantum hypothesis testing
papers.authors: Mark M. Wilde
papers.abstract: How many independent quantum systems does it take to hide one system that is correlated with a reference? An observer can measure all the systems together with the reference to detect the correlation. We turn any such measurement into binary tests on a single system and the reference. For each test we bound the probability of declaring a signal when an independent pair was prepared. Averaging the largest signal acceptance probabilities allowed by these bounds controls the normalized trace distance in the convex-split lemma. A second bound gives a sufficient number of systems by minimizing the hypothesis-testing relative entropy over the state of the reference. Both bounds hold for density operators on separable Hilbert spaces. Comparing two distributions for the location of the hidden system gives one-shot bounds for private communication and one-way secret key distillation, including the public information available to an eavesdropper. For a fixed finite-alphabet model with separable quantum outputs and positive information advantage and variances, we recover the known Gaussian corrections to the attainable number of private or key bits from $n$ independent repetitions and bound the remaining loss by $\log_2 n+O(1)$ at fixed errors. The position-based key distillation protocol attains this bound with $O(n)$ public bits.

papers.title: AIstatLab at BraTS-GoAT 2026 Task 3: Quality-Controlled Consensus Pseudo-Labeling and Dense Expert Adaptation
papers.authors: Heeseung Shin; Changwon Lim
papers.abstract: BraTS-GoAT Task 3 evaluates brain-tumor segmentation across heterogeneous entities using shared ET, TC, and WT regions. We present a 3D ResidualEncoderUNet trained with quality-controlled consensus pseudo-labels, a training-only nested-region objective, and a four-expert bottleneck adapter. Five-fold ResEnc-M/L teachers gener ated predictions for 1,138 unlabeled cases; fusion, hierarchy enforcement, and confidence-and-agreement screening retained 983 for training with 1,351 annotated cases. The final five-fold ResEnc-M entry achieved mean DSC 0.834, mean NSD 0.510, and Acalc = 0.6720 on the validation server. Component effects were modest and region-dependent, with the clearest gains on ET. Source code is available at https://github.com/HeeSeung-Shin/Brats2026-Goat-HS.

papers.title: Stereo Visual Odometry with In-the-Loop Geometric Feed-Forward Models Towards Dense Metric Mapping
papers.authors: Fahira Afzal Maken; Sagun Man Singh Shrestha; Edward Vanderfeen; Lucas Carvalho de Lima; Rongxin Li et al.
papers.abstract: We present a stereo visual odometry (SVO) framework that integrates geometric feed-forward models (GFMs) for dense depth prediction with factor-graph-based visual odometry to achieve accurate localisation and dense metric mapping. Our key idea is to exploit sparse but reliable metric geometry estimated from stereo and temporal multi-view observations to calibrate dense GFM predictions, while retaining the robustness and efficiency of model-based SVO. Rather than directly conditioning the GFM on potentially noisy stereo depth, optimised 3D landmarks are used to jointly estimate a scale-shift transformation over all keyframes within each local submap, yielding metrically consistent dense depth predictions. To balance accuracy and computational efficiency, we introduce a hierarchical factor-graph architecture. At the local level, sliding-window optimisation estimates high-frequency camera poses and multi-view-refined 3D landmarks. Dense predictions are generated only for selected keyframes and registered within each submap using SE(3) Generalised ICP. Consecutive submaps are further aligned in Sim(3) using their shared geometry, allowing residual scale inconsistencies to be corrected. These intra- and inter-submap constraints are incorporated into a global factor graph to produce a consistent trajectory and dense metric reconstruction. Extensive experiments on public and in-house datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves competitive odometry accuracy against geometric and learning-based baselines while providing accurate dense metric reconstruction and improved robustness to failures in learned depth prediction.

papers.title: High-Dimensional Structured Light Tomography with a Tilted Lens
papers.authors: Altilano C. Barbosa; Isaac Tribaldo; Amanda K. Fritsch; Marcos G. de Oliveira; Gabriel Molina-Terriza et al.
papers.abstract: In this work, we investigate high-dimensional spatial mode tomography using intensity measurements and the astigmatic transformation implemented with a tilted lens. We improve the method previously published in Ref. [1] to perform the spatial tomography not restricted to a fixed order, which allowed us to achieve good fidelity for a mode space dimension as high as $D=66\,$. Since the literature is not unanimous, we also present a comprehensive revision of light propagation through a tilted lens for an accurate description of the transformation used for tomography. We derive its effective focal lengths, and analyze its role as an astigmatic mode converter. Moreover, we establish its explicit domain of validity within the Hermite-Gaussian basis.

papers.title: MIR-Depth: Multi-Range Refinement for Single-View RGB-D Depth Completion of Transparent Objects
papers.authors: Xinzhe Fu; Qi Shao; Yuanfei Xie; Taoyu Wu; Zhihao Cao et al.
papers.abstract: Recovering accurate visible-surface depth from a single RGB-D image and an object mask is essential for robotic grasping and manipulation of transparent objects. Specular reflections cause missing depth, while refraction corrupts nonzero returns with background depth, making raw measurements unreliable as surface anchors. Under a fixed sampling budget, refining an initial single-view prediction within a single search interval either misses large refraction offsets or sacrifices fine local resolution. To resolve this single-view trade-off, MIR-Depth constructs Coordinate-Aware Multi-Range Hypotheses: a 3D-aggregated global inverse-depth volume and depth-axis-filtered pixel-wise local volumes around a prior-guided initial depth. Selective Recurrent Refinement then introduces out-of-bounds lookup masking and validity-masked softmax fusion to iteratively update inverse depth from these volumes using a multi-scale ConvGRU. Finally, Spatially Gated Correction applies a learned per-pixel spatial gate to the full-resolution residual, preserving accurate initial geometry without imposing raw sensor readings as hard constraints. Experiments on TransCG, TODD, TRansPose, ClearPose, and HouseCat6D show that MIR-Depth achieves lower error than ReMake, DFNet, BP-Net, and PSD. Real-robot evaluations confirm accurate surface geometry for 6-DoF grasp pose prediction. Code and pretrained models will be publicly available.

papers.title: Watertight Mesh Optimization of Textured Objects
papers.authors: Nathaniel Burgdorfer; Philippos Mordohai
papers.abstract: When reconstructing high-quality 3D assets from images, existing approaches often excel at one objective while compromising another, and frequently overlook the intrinsic quality of the reconstructed surfaces. We present MODL, a framework that jointly optimizes geometry and view-dependent appearance directly on a watertight triangle mesh. Our approach combines Laplacian-preconditioned optimization for smooth vertex updates with curvature-adaptive remeshing to preserve fine details and well-shaped triangles. The triangle mesh is optimized subject to multi-view normalized cross-correlation constraints, but without segmentation, geometric supervision or alpha-blending. Evaluations on object reconstruction datasets demonstrate that MODL achieves competitive novel-view synthesis while producing geometrically accurate models with superior intrinsic mesh quality. Our results highlight the potential of direct mesh optimization to unify photorealistic rendering, geometric reconstruction, and practical 3D asset creation.

papers.title: Single-fit inference for the realized prediction error of a logistic model with many predictors
papers.authors: Seyoung Park; Eun Ryung Lee
papers.abstract: When independent validation data are unavailable, evaluating a fitted logistic model on new patients requires estimating prediction error and uncertainty. Evaluating the fit on training data is often optimistic. Bootstrap validation is widely used to correct this bias, but with many predictors, it can retain bias and yield unreliable confidence intervals. In this article, we study these limitations and develop single-fit estimation and inference without resampling. When the number of Gaussian predictors grows proportionally with sample size, we analyze unpenalized logistic models. We prove that standard bootstrap correction can have nonzero limiting bias even as the resample count grows and location-shifted intervals can have zero limiting coverage. Instead, we adjust the fitted scores to consistently estimate realized Brier and log losses. We account for common fitting and adjustment error to construct valid marginal intervals and joint regions. We also establish these single-fit estimation and inference guarantees for certain non-Gaussian designs in proportional dimensions. Under moderate dimension growth and possible misspecification with general predictors, we extend single-fit inference to ridge regularization and construct asymptotically valid confidence intervals for realized log loss. Simulations and analyses of hospital and diabetes datasets support our theory and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods.

papers.title: Affine Boosted Gauss Curvature Flow
papers.authors: Andrews. Ben; Rajpal. Devesh
papers.abstract: We prove convexity in the affine orbit of entropies associated to Gauss curvature flow for sub-affine powers. This allows the construction of an affine boosted Gauss curvature flow, which keeps the evolving hypersurface at the affine minimizer of the Gaussian entropy. The modified flow has bounded isoperimetric ratio, and after rescaling it converges along a sequence of times to self-similar solutions of the Gauss curvature flow. The construction also proves existence of new self-similar solutions to Gauss curvature flow in the sub-affine regime.

papers.title: TuringSpace: Grounding Spatial Intelligence in Action with Interactive CAPTCHAs
papers.authors: Xuwei Ding; Skylar Zhai; Linxin Song; Jiarui Feng; Dongqi Fu et al.
papers.abstract: Humans act in the visual world by inferring the 3D layout behind a 2D view, predicting how an action changes it, and correcting themselves after seeing the result. Can multimodal large language models (MLLMs) do the same? CAPTCHAs offer a natural test, since humans solve them through this very loop, clicking and dragging on the screen and adjusting after each result. Yet existing CAPTCHA benchmarks are largely solved and rarely spatial, while spatial benchmarks rarely require action. We therefore present TuringSpace, a synthetic web environment of 125 interactive CAPTCHAs that span five spatial abilities and must be solved through clicks and drags on the screen. Every task is a program that generates new instances with a checker and an oracle, so the tasks also form a scalable training gym. Humans solve 94.1% of the tasks, whereas the best model, GPT-6 Astra, still fails 25.9% of them, and the best open-weight model, Kimi K3, fails 68.0%. Our further analysis shows that most failures come from misreading the screenshot, and that model reasoning rarely corrects a wrong belief but hallucinates evidence to defend it. To test whether such spatial abilities can be learned, we fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B on this gym. Its success rate rises from 1.6% to 33.1%, above Kimi K3, and it improves on all seven out-of-distribution benchmarks, including a 9.9-point gain on the real-world indoor videos of VSI-Bench. These results show that grounding spatial intelligence in screen actions exposes what MLLMs lack and offers a scalable way to teach it, with gains that transfer to real-world scenes. We will release TuringSpace to support further study.

papers.title: A GPU Interior-Point Solver with Macro-Element Condensation for Equilibrium-Based Plasticity
papers.authors: Youssef Essousy; Mohammed-Khalil Ferradi
papers.abstract: Equilibrium-based conic formulations of elastoplasticity and limit analysis provide statically admissible stress fields but generate large Newton systems whose sparse factorization limits three-dimensional computations. This work develops and analyzes a macro-element condensation tailored to the Newton systems arising from primal--dual interior-point methods. Exploiting four-tetrahedron macro-elements, the method eliminates stress directions and macro-internal traction-continuity multipliers, yielding reduced systems that can be solved using positive-definite factorizations, with estimated reductions of approximately \(4\times\) in dimension and structural nonzeros relative to stress-only elimination. The validity of this elimination is established through global and macro-local nonsingularity conditions. Local nonsingularity is independent of the yield criterion in elastoplasticity, whereas in limit analysis it holds directly for Rankine and is ensured for von Mises through trace-bound augmentation. Numerical results show that, relative to stress-only elimination, the proposed condensation achieves CPU speedups of up to approximately \(2\times\) and reduces peak linear-solver memory by up to \(66.5\%\). We further develop a CUDA Fortran implementation that exploits uniform macro-local blocks through batched routines and uses cuDSS for the reduced sparse solve. This implementation achieves speedups of up to \(13.5\times\) over its CPU counterpart and up to \(87.5\times\) over MOSEK, while successfully solving the largest tested 3D problems that exceed the device-memory capacity of the GPU solver CuClarabel. For elastoplasticity, we also propose a preconditioned conjugate-gradient solver that reduces device-memory requirements relative to the direct GPU solver, at the expense of increased solution time.

papers.title: Causal Discovery with False Positive Error Control
papers.authors: Erik Jahn; Venkat Chandrasekaran; Frederick Eberhardt; Leonard Schulman
papers.abstract: Causal discovery methods produce data-driven hypotheses about causal relationships, which may become new scientific findings or inform decisions about downstream interventions. In such settings, false positive causal claims can be more consequential than false negatives. Yet few methods target false positive error control in causal discovery, and existing error guarantees are often asymptotic and require strong versions of the faithfulness assumption. We introduce the $m$-conservative PC algorithm and prove that it controls false discovery rate in the linear Gaussian setting under an extremely weak version of the faithfulness assumption. In our framework, false positive error for causal graphs is defined based on the conditional-independence information they entail, yielding a metric that penalizes both false adjacencies and incorrect edge orientations. The parameter $m$ quantifies a trade-off between algorithmic complexity and the strength of the required faithfulness assumption. The $m$-conservative PC algorithm combines undirected graph learning, a Benjamini-Yekutieli-style procedure for conditional independence testing, and a conservative orientation step that marks unresolved or contradictory edge directions as ambiguous. Our algorithm produces valid outputs and retains error guarantees even in the finite-sample setting, despite possible random errors in the conditional independence tests.

papers.title: Data-Driven Hamiltonian Under Parametric Uncertainty
papers.authors: Zach Liu; Namhoon Cho; Jason J. Choi
papers.abstract: Hamilton--Jacobi (HJ) reachability computes the states from which a system can be kept out of an unsafe region, but it requires knowledge of dynamics. The data-driven Hamiltonian (DDH), under a black-box dynamics setting, lower bounds the Hamiltonian directly from trajectory data, which produces a guaranteed conservative safe set. However, it needs a Lipschitz constant of the dynamics, and its bound loosens with the distance from the data. We consider dynamics that are linear in unknown parameters through a known feature vector, with a Gaussian prior on the parameters, and use this structure to construct a parametric DDH. From a few short trajectories with noisy velocity measurements, the parametric DDH lower-bounds the Hamiltonian at all states and costates with a probability of at least $1-δ$. The safe set obtained by replacing the Hamiltonian with this bound is then contained in the true safe set with the same probability. For control-affine systems, evaluating the bound amounts to a second-order cone program, so it can be solved efficiently within existing grid-based and neural PDE solvers. We demonstrate the approach on a two-state system and a six-state lunar lander.

papers.title: SceneAnything: Agentic Reconstruction of Large-Scale Mesh Scenes from a Single Video
papers.authors: Bowen Xue; Saeed Hadadan; Fabrice Rousselle; Zahra Montazeri; Ravi Ramamoorthi et al.
papers.abstract: Reconstructing an editable 3D scene from video requires matching visible structure while plausibly completing unseen surfaces. Agents can write scene-construction programs, but direct reconstruction attempts often produce errors in layout, scale, and lighting. We introduce SceneAnything, an automated system for reconstructing mesh scenes from real and generated videos, enabling text-to-scene construction when paired with video generation. A software harness coordinates agents, pretrained vision models, and graphics tools through an explicit reconstruction protocol. Shared camera, depth, and segmentation estimates ground component construction: a scene-owner agent plans the environment and briefs authors, who write parameterized Blender programs. A visibility- and fit-based level-of-detail rule selects the construction level, while unseen regions are completed and marked as inferred. Assembled scenes use fitted lighting and supported motion, and revisions undergo programmatic checks and independent visual comparisons. Accepted programs and lessons are reused across scenes. We evaluate on 100 scenes; subset comparisons show improved original-view fidelity over direct-agent reconstruction and higher novel-view content similarity than the compared video-to-3D methods. We will release the harness, agent instructions, reusable libraries, and scenes.

papers.title: VideoRNG: Relightable Neural Gaussians from Generative Video Models
papers.authors: Bowen Xue; Saeed Hadadan; Fabrice Rousselle; Ravi Ramamoorthi; Zahra Montazeri et al.
papers.abstract: Generating realistic 3D assets remains constrained by classical representations: surface meshes and compact physically based materials struggle to express objects whose appearance arises from fine geometry or complex light transport, while existing Gaussian-splatting generators typically bake fixed illumination into appearance. We introduce VideoRNG, a two-stage method that generates complete, relightable 3D assets from a text prompt or a single image without prescribing a mesh or analytic material model. A video generator fine-tuned from a pretrained video diffusion backbone first produces a structured RGBA turntable sequence under a known pose, camera, and illumination. A feed-forward large reconstruction model initialized from a pretrained video diffusion backbone then maps the video-VAE latent frames of selected turntable frames directly to millions of anisotropic Gaussians with learned neural appearance features. A shared directional decoder and stochastic Gaussian ray tracer turn this representation, which we call ray-traced Relightable Neural Gaussians (rtRNG), into radiance under novel viewpoints and illumination. To preserve high-frequency appearance while learning geometry, we introduce depth-anchored appearance training, and we make million-Gaussian reconstruction practical through foreground token selection and cost-aware distributed sampling. VideoRNG generates complex assets such as fur, feathers, and spider webs that can be interactively rendered, relit, and integrated into scenes.

papers.title: MoRE: Mixture-of-Experts for Multi-Physics Robotic World Models
papers.authors: Ziyu Zhu; Shaowei Liu; Albert J. Zhai; Henry Che; Wei-Chiu Ma et al.
papers.abstract: A robotic world model should predict how objects evolve under robot actions and physical dynamics. While recent 3D world models have shown strong predictive capabilities, they still struggle with the heterogeneous dynamics arising from diverse object interactions. To address this in a unified framework, we decompose robotic interactions into distinct physical regimes and assign each to a specialized motion expert. We introduce MoRE, a 3D world model with a mixture of motion experts organized around rigid, deformable, and prehensile dynamics. This design enables a single model to capture diverse physical behaviors while preserving regime-specific priors. Trained on mixed simulation and real-world data, MoRE integrates with Model Predictive Control (MPC) to support diverse manipulation tasks. Experiments show that MoRE improves prediction accuracy across physics regimes, leading to stronger real-world MPC performance. Code, data, and project website are available at https://alwaysleepy.github.io/MoRE-WM-site/.

papers.title: Breaking Noise Shortcuts in Self-Supervised Learning Via Noise-Aligned View Generation
papers.authors: Oankar R. Patil; May D. Wang
papers.abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) is increasingly applied to scientific imaging domains, such as microscopy, where labels are scarce but noisy data is abundant. These domains exhibit significant signal-dependent noise, which can create a representational shortcut: since both augmented views derive from the same noisy image, the encoder can boost view agreement by also encoding noise patterns rather than semantic content. To enable noise-robust representation learning without knowledge of underlying noise models, we introduce Self-Aligned Noise Augmentation (SEANA), a drop-in module that generates noise-aware SSL views. SEANA learns an invertible variance-stabilizing transform (VST) from noisy data, then estimates the clean signal and resamples independent noise in learned VST space, requiring no clean targets, no dataset-specific denoiser training or use at inference, and no changes to the SSL objective or encoder. On CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-100 under synthetic Gaussian, Poisson-Gaussian, and multiplicative noise, SEANA improves clean-test linear-probe accuracy across contrastive/non-contrastive SSL methods, indicating higher-quality representations. On real fluorescence imaging, SEANA improves Jurkat cell-cycle stage classification by up to 28.6pp over standard SSL and 27.5pp over denoiser-preprocessed baselines. In all settings, SEANA outperforms the denoiser-preprocessed SSL pipelines, demonstrating that learned VST-space noise-aligned resampling yields more robust representations than denoising alone. Code is available at: https://github.com/opatil31/SEANA

papers.title: Gaussian Quasi-Likelihood Estimation for Nonsynchronously Observed Lévy processes
papers.authors: Teppei Ogihara; Yuma Uehara
papers.abstract: We study parametric inference for a two-dimensional simple Lévy process observed at high frequency over an expanding time horizon, where the two components are sampled in a possibly non-synchronous manner. Combining Gaussian quasi-likelihood estimation for Lévy SDEs with the non-synchronous quasi-likelihood methodology, we construct a Gaussian-type quasi-likelihood based on the covariance structure of non-synchronous increments, and we prove consistency and asymptotic normality of the resulting estimators. The convergence rates coincide with those in the synchronous setting, while the asymptotic variance depends essentially on the sampling design and becomes more complicated under non-synchronicity. To handle the different moment structure of pure-jump Lévy processes, we introduce an additional convergence assumption and provide tractable sufficient conditions linked to the observation scheme. Numerical experiments illustrate the finite-sample performance of the proposed estimators.

papers.title: When Should Deployed BCI Decoders Adapt? A Resource-Priced Ladder for Frozen EEG Trunks
